title: Skin Cancer: Types, Diagnosis, and Management
subject: Pathology
summary: Skin cancer involves uncontrolled growth of abnormal skin cells, primarily caused by UV radiation exposure. It encompasses various types, with basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and melanoma being the most common. Early diagnosis and appropriate management are crucial for improved outcomes.

sections.p: Skin cancer is the uncontrolled proliferation of abnormal cells originating from the skin. Diagnosis typically begins with clinical suspicion based on visual inspection of suspicious lesions, followed by histological confirmation via biopsy. The three main types are basal cell carcinoma (BCC), squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), and melanoma.
b: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC): Most common skin cancer, often presents as a pearly nodule with rolled edges and telangiectasias, commonly on sun-exposed areas.
Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC): Second most common, often appears as a scaly, red patch or nodule, sometimes ulcerated, with potential for metastasis.
Melanoma: Least common but most aggressive, arising from melanocytes, characterized by irregular borders, asymmetry, varied color, and increasing size (ABCDE criteria).
Kaposi's sarcoma (KS): A vascular tumor, often associated with HIV/AIDS, presenting as purple-brown patches, plaques, or nodules, particularly in immunocompromised individuals.

sections.p: Staging systems are used to assess the extent of skin cancer, guiding treatment and prognosis. While BCC rarely metastasizes and is usually staged locally, SCC and especially melanoma require more comprehensive staging.
b: Basal Cell Carcinoma: Generally staged based on size, location, and presence of aggressive histological features; rarely metastasizes.
Squamous Cell Carcinoma: Staged using the TNM (Tumor, Node, Metastasis) system, considering tumor size, depth, perineural invasion, and regional lymph node involvement.

Melanoma: Staged using the AJCC (American Joint Committee on Cancer) TNM system, which includes tumor thickness (Breslow depth), ulceration, mitotic rate, lymph node involvement, and distant metastasis.
Kaposi's Sarcoma: Staged based on tumor extent, immune status (CD4 count), and presence of systemic illness (TIS staging).

sections.p: The primary cause of most skin cancers is exposure to ultraviolet (UV) radiation from sunlight. Other factors, including genetic predisposition and immunosuppression, also play significant roles.
b: UV radiation: Damages DNA in skin cells, leading to mutations; accounts for increasing incidence of BCC, SCC, and melanoma.
Fair skin type: Individuals with less melanin are more susceptible to UV damage.
Genetic predisposition: Family history of melanoma or certain genetic syndromes (e.g., xeroderma pigmentosum) increase risk.
Immunosuppression: Conditions like HIV/AIDS or organ transplantation increase risk, particularly for SCC and Kaposi's sarcoma.
Chronic irritation/inflammation: Non-healing wounds, scars, or chronic ulcers can predispose to SCC.
Chemical exposure: Certain industrial chemicals (e.g., arsenic) are associated with increased risk.

sections.p: Skin cancers present with a wide range of appearances, making careful visual inspection crucial. Clinicians should be vigilant for any new, changing, or non-healing skin lesions.
b: Basal cell carcinoma: Pearly papule or nodule with rolled borders, often with central ulceration (rodent ulcer) and telangiectasias; commonly on face, neck, or hands.
Squamous cell carcinoma: Red, scaly patch or nodule, often crusted or ulcerated; may be tender; common on sun-exposed areas like lips, ears, scalp, or hands.
Melanoma: Asymmetrical lesion with irregular borders, varied color (black, brown, red, white, blue), and diameter greater than 6mm; often evolving in size, shape, or color.
Kaposi's sarcoma: Purple, brown, or black macules, papules, plaques, or nodules; can be solitary or multiple, often on lower extremities, face, or oral mucosa; may involve internal organs.

sections.p: Investigations aim to confirm the diagnosis, determine the type of cancer, assess its depth and spread, and guide treatment. Biopsy is the cornerstone of diagnosis.

To obtain tissue for histological examination and confirm the diagnosis, determine the type of skin cancer, and assess depth of invasion. An excisional biopsy is preferred for suspected melanoma if feasible, ensuring clear margins. If biopsy is not possible, clinical follow-up and referral are critical.

To provide definitive diagnosis, classify the tumor type (BCC, SCC, melanoma, KS), assess tumor thickness (Breslow depth for melanoma), mitotic rate, ulceration, and presence of aggressive features. This is crucial for staging and treatment planning.
To assess for regional lymphadenopathy, indicating potential metastatic spread, especially for SCC and melanoma. Palpation of regional lymph nodes is a standard part of the physical exam.

For intermediate to high-risk melanoma and some SCCs, to detect microscopic metastasis to regional lymph nodes. Identifies the first lymph node(s) to which cancer cells are most likely to spread. Often unavailable in low-resource settings; clinical follow-up and imaging become more critical.

sections.p: Recognizing red flags is crucial for early intervention. Complications vary by cancer type but can include local destruction, disfigurement, and metastasis.
b: Rapid growth or change in a lesion's appearance (size, shape, color).
Bleeding, itching, or pain in a skin lesion.
Non-healing ulcer or sore.
Enlarged regional lymph nodes.
Local tissue destruction and disfigurement, especially with advanced BCC or SCC.
Metastasis to distant organs (brain, lung, liver, bone) in advanced melanoma or SCC, leading to organ dysfunction.
Immunosuppression-related complications in Kaposi's sarcoma (e.g., opportunistic infections).

sections.p: Management depends on the type, stage, and location of the skin cancer, as well as patient factors. Surgical excision is the primary treatment for most localized skin cancers.
b: Surgical excision: Standard treatment for BCC, SCC, and melanoma; aims for complete removal with clear margins. Mohs micrographic surgery for high-risk BCC/SCC in cosmetically sensitive areas.
Radiotherapy: Used for BCC and SCC in patients unsuitable for surgery, or as adjuvant therapy for advanced disease or positive margins.
Topical therapies: Imiquimod cream or 5-fluorouracil cream for superficial BCC or SCC in situ, especially in low-risk areas.
Cryotherapy: Freezing with liquid nitrogen for small, superficial BCCs or SCC in situ, particularly in low-resource settings where surgery may be limited.
Systemic therapy: Chemotherapy, targeted therapy (e.g., BRAF inhibitors for melanoma), or immunotherapy (e.g., PD-1 inhibitors) for advanced or metastatic melanoma and some SCCs.

Antiretroviral therapy (ART): Essential for managing Kaposi's sarcoma in HIV-positive individuals, often leading to regression of lesions. Chemotherapy or local therapies may be added for extensive or symptomatic KS.

sections.p: Regular follow-up is crucial for early detection of recurrence or new primary lesions. Prevention focuses on reducing UV exposure.
b: Regular skin self-examinations: Patients should be taught to check their skin monthly for new or changing lesions.
Clinical follow-up: Frequent skin checks by a clinician, especially for patients with a history of skin cancer, tailored to risk.
Sun protection: Avoid peak sun hours, wear protective clothing, use broad-spectrum sunscreen (SPF 30 or higher).
Education: Counsel patients on risk factors and the importance of early detection.
Immunosuppression management: For Kaposi's sarcoma, optimizing ART adherence and immune status is key.

sections.p: Many benign skin lesions can mimic skin cancer, making accurate diagnosis challenging. Careful clinical assessment and dermoscopy are vital.
b: Seborrheic keratosis: Benign, waxy, 'stuck-on' appearance, often pigmented; can be confused with melanoma or pigmented BCC.
Actinic keratosis: Precancerous lesion, rough, scaly patch on sun-exposed skin; can progress to SCC.
Benign nevus (mole): Usually symmetrical, uniform color, regular borders; can be confused with melanoma.
Dermatofibroma: Firm, often pigmented nodule that dimples when squeezed; can be confused with BCC or melanoma.
Pyogenic granuloma: Rapidly growing, red, friable papule that bleeds easily; can be confused with amelanotic melanoma or SCC.
Lichen planus or psoriasis: Inflammatory skin conditions that can present with scaly plaques, sometimes mimicking SCC.

sections.p: Certain factors can lead to misinterpretation of clinical findings or diagnostic tests, potentially delaying or misguiding management.
b: Inadequate biopsy: A superficial or partial biopsy may miss the true depth or aggressive features of a lesion, leading to under-staging.
Amelanotic melanoma: Lacks pigment, making it difficult to recognize clinically and often mistaken for benign lesions or other skin cancers.
Inflamed lesions: Inflammation can obscure typical features of skin cancer, making diagnosis challenging.
Location: Lesions in hidden areas (e.g., scalp, soles of feet, nail beds) may be overlooked or diagnosed late.
Lack of dermoscopy expertise: Without dermoscopy, subtle features of early melanoma or other skin cancers can be missed.
Limited access to histopathology: In low-resource settings, delays in processing or lack of expert pathologists can hinder accurate diagnosis.

whenToSeekHelp: Any new or changing skin lesion that bleeds, itches, or is painful.
A non-healing sore or ulcer on the skin.
Enlarged lymph nodes, especially in the drainage area of a suspicious skin lesion.
Systemic symptoms like unexplained weight loss, fatigue, or persistent cough in a patient with known skin cancer.

faq.q: What is the most common type of skin cancer?
faq.a: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common type of skin cancer, accounting for about 80% of all cases. It is locally invasive but rarely metastasizes.

faq.q: How can I tell if a mole is cancerous?
faq.a: Use the ABCDE rule: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variation, Diameter greater than 6mm, and Evolving (changing) size, shape, or color. Any mole showing these features should be evaluated by a clinician.

faq.q: Is sun exposure the only cause of skin cancer?
faq.a: No, while UV radiation from sun exposure is the primary cause for most skin cancers, other factors like genetic predisposition, immunosuppression (e.g., HIV/AIDS for Kaposi's sarcoma), and chronic irritation can also contribute.

exam: A 65-year-old farmer presents with a non-healing ulcer on his lower lip that has been present for 8 months and is slowly growing. What is your primary differential diagnosis and what is your immediate next step? — Primary differential is squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) given the chronic sun exposure, location, and non-healing nature. Immediate next step is an incisional biopsy of the lesion to confirm diagnosis and assess depth.

What is the most likely diagnosis, and what is its metastatic potential compared to other skin cancers? — Most likely diagnosis is basal cell carcinoma (BCC). BCC has very low metastatic potential, almost never metastasizing, unlike squamous cell carcinoma (which has moderate potential) and melanoma (which has high metastatic potential).

A patient with a history of multiple basal cell carcinomas asks about prevention. What key advice would you give them regarding sun protection? — Advise avoiding peak sun hours (10 am to 4 pm), wearing protective clothing (long sleeves, wide-brimmed hats), seeking shade, and regularly applying broad-spectrum sunscreen with an SPF of 30 or higher, reapplying every 2 hours or after swimming/sweating.

What are the 'red flags' that would prompt you to urgently refer a patient with a skin lesion for specialist assessment? — Red flags include rapid growth or change in size/shape/color of a lesion, bleeding or persistent non-healing ulceration, new onset itching or pain in a lesion, and palpable regional lymphadenopathy associated with a suspicious skin lesion.

Distinguish between actinic keratosis and squamous cell carcinoma. Why is this distinction clinically important? — Actinic keratosis (AK) is a precancerous lesion, a rough, scaly patch on sun-exposed skin, representing atypical keratinocytes confined to the epidermis. Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is an invasive malignancy where atypical keratinocytes have breached the basement membrane.
